title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
body: Plenty from China yesterday: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: dollar softer ahead of US CPI --- The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: US inflation is becoming less widespread, and that matters more than the headline rate suggests
body: US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August and a touch above expectations of 3.6%, according to Wednesday's Consumer Price Index report. Prices climbed 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose to 2.6% from 2.4%, slightly above the 2.5% expected, with a monthly gain of around 0.3%. On the surface, that is not the direction the Federal Reserve wants. But Bloomberg Economics read the report as less troubling than the headline numbers suggest. Anna Wong, its chief US economist, highlighted a measure of how widespread inflation is, rather than how fast it is running on average, and noted that it fell in September. It's an interesting lens on the data, and one that may carry more weight than usual. Wong said the gauge is built in a similar way to an inflation breadth measure based on PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation index, which she linked to Fed chair Kevin Warsh. What inflation "diffusion" means The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is built from hundreds of separate price categories, from rent and car insurance to eggs and airfares. The headline inflation rate is effectively a weighted average of all of them. A diffusion, or breadth, measure takes a different approach. Instead of averaging, it counts. Bloomberg Economics' version asks what share of CPI components are rising faster than 3% a year. It tracks that share over two windows.

title: Stablecoins have stopped growing. So why is usage still rising?
body: Standard Chartered now expects the stablecoin market to reach $2 trillion by 2030, two years later than it first projected. The bank made the change after total stablecoin supply stalled at roughly $309 billion this year, according to Cointelegraph, which was shown the report. Read quickly, a "$2 trillion" headline sounds bullish. It is really a delay. The more interesting part of the report is the bank's argument that stablecoins are still being used more, even though the market has stopped getting bigger. Understanding how both can be true is one of the most useful ideas in crypto right now. Market size and usage are two different things A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar, backed by reserves held by the issuer. Because each token is meant to be worth $1, a stablecoin's market capitalisation is in practice the number of tokens in circulation. That figure tells you how many stablecoin dollars exist. It does not tell you how hard those dollars are working. Think of a taxi fleet. The number of cars on the road can stay flat while the number of trips rises, because each car is busier. Geoffrey Kendrick, Standard Chartered's head of digital assets research, describes stablecoins in the same terms: supply growth has slowed, but existing tokens are changing hands more often as their uses widen. Economists call this velocity. The practical point for readers is that a flat market cap chart, on its own, does not show demand fading.

title: US stocks might have a bigger problem than just hotter inflation

Tech shares were the ones bearing the brunt of the pain and with futures also pointing lower today, it is tempting to pin all the blame on inflation. The simple argument is that the last thing that investors want to see is the Fed reaching for another reason to keep rates "higher for longer". Having said that, the bond market reaction didn't exactly play to the same tune. Treasury yields spiked higher on the data release but quickly gave it all back and are falling even lower today. 10-year yields are now down to 5.10%, its lowest in three weeks. And yet, stocks seem to be struggling still. So, what gives? If higher borrowing costs were supposed to be the main concern for equities, shouldn't the pullback in yields offer some relief instead? Besides, the market pricing for the October Fed meeting hasn't shifted all that much too. Traders are pricing in roughly 29% odds of a rate hike, just a mild step up from around 22% odds yesterday. While hotter inflation certainly isn't helping with market sentiment, it is not entirely convincing to say that the report yesterday tells the whole story behind the selling. title: RBNZ Signals Flexibility Amid Inflation Pressures
body: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Chief Economist Paul Conway said Thursday that the late-October interest rate decision remains "completely open," despite ongoing inflation pressures. Speaking at IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, he emphasized the need for flexibility: "We want the option of either holding steady or raising rates by 25 basis points, and I believe we currently have that option." Conway reiterated that an increase in the official cash rate (OCR) is still considered "most likely," although the timing has not yet been determined. He pointed out that the recent decline in oil prices and in the New Zealand dollar has created additional short-term upward pressure on inflation, complicating the near-term outlook. Nevertheless, the RBNZ continues to expect inflation to return to its 1–3% target range next year, even if current conditions remain challenging in the short term. title: China 10Y Yield at Over 1-Year Low
body: China's 10-year government bond yield fell to around 1.65% on Thursday, its lowest level since May 2025, as a strengthening yuan and a sluggish domestic economy boosted demand for sovereign debt. The yield has dropped 18 basis points since the end of December, and over the past 12 months Chinese government bonds have generated nearly 10% returns for dollar-based investors. They have also been supported by China's relative insulation from rising oil prices, underpinned by sizable strategic reserves and an ongoing shift toward electrified transportation. In addition, Beijing's initiatives to attract more foreign participation in its onshore bond market are providing further backing as China works to enhance the yuan's international role. The rally has pushed the yield differential between Chinese and US government bonds to a record this month, with China's 10-year yield at 1.67%, standing 352 basis points below that of comparable-maturity US Treasuries. It's interesting that stocks, copper, crypto, the US dollar and yields are all trading lower today, while gold has regained all the losses. It feels more like a stagflationary environment where risk assets and the US dollar generally underperform, while gold outperforms. Looking ahead, we have the Flash PMIs, the FOMC, the US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections as key catalysts. If the economic data starts pointing to deteriorating economic conditions, then we could see the market getting increasingly worried about growth. This would be negative for risk sentiment and could further weigh on Bitcoin and the crypto market in general. What could change the picture completely would be an end to the US-Iran war, as that would immediately improve the growth outlook. title: US inflation worries aren't over yet as PPI and retail sales pose fresh risks for markets
body: The hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday was already enough to give markets a bit of a headache. And despite the initial surge higher in Treasury yields fading, there's still evidence of jitters with equities staying under pressure today. So if investors are hoping for some breathing room to get by, I'm afraid there might be more bad news to deal with as we're not quite done with the inflation and economic data risks just yet. Looking to the session ahead, there are three key US economic data releases to watch out for: September PPI: This will be another inflation test, this time looking at price pressures faced by producers September retail sales: This will be a key gauge of consumer spending and whether higher prices are actually slowing demand Weekly initial jobless claims: This will be a timely check on whether the US labour market is starting to show more signs of weakness Given the backdrop this week, I'd argue that the PPI and retail sales will carry the bigger risks for markets. A hot PPI reading later will only add to inflation concerns after the stronger consumer price numbers seen yesterday. It could offer an indication that price pressures are proving to be more stubborn than the Fed would like. And if retail sales also surprises to the upside, that could stir up a potentially uncomfortable combination for the Fed to deal with.

title: Gold whipsaws after US CPI as data falls short of bringing an October rate hike back into play

I think the initial reaction was an overreaction, as I mentioned that an uptick to 0.3% wouldn't have been enough to make the market to fully price in an October rate hike. In fact, after the knee-jerk reaction, the probability of a rate hike at the upcoming meeting stabilised around 30%, just 9% higher than the 21% probability seen before the CPI release. Today, we have US PPI on the agenda, but I don't see it materially changing rate hike expectations. As a result, we could see a similar market reaction to yesterday's CPI release, unless PPI surprises to the downside, in which case gold could stage a relief rally. On the geopolitical front, not much has changed. The Saudi Arabia–Houthi conflict continues, while US–Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. Meanwhile, oil prices continue to rise amid the ongoing Middle East crisis. Looking ahead, the focus will remain on developments in the Middle East and the Fed's policy outlook. A breakthrough in US–Iran negotiations could trigger a strong rally in gold, as traders would scale back rate hike expectations. A Fed that is slow to respond to rising inflation could also support gold if inflation expectations rise faster than nominal yields, pushing real yields lower.

title: France inflation rises sharply in September as price pressures add to ECB rate hike dilemma
body: France September final CPI +3.1% vs +3.0% y/y prelim Prior +2.4% France September final HICP +3.4% vs +3.4% y/y prelim Prior +2.6% France September core CPI +1.5% y/y Prior +1.1% The final figures for September are out and they're not exactly offering much comfort for the ECB. The annual readings confirm another notable jump in price pressures, adding to the inflation concerns we've been seeing across the euro area lately. Energy prices remain the biggest culprit, surging 21.3% annually in September compared with 16.7% in August. Once again, that is largely triggered by the ongoing fallout from the Middle East conflict. That being said, we're also starting to see broader price pressures creeping in elsewhere. Core annual inflation picked up to 1.5% from 1.1% previously, helped by a notable jump in services inflation - which rose to 2.4% from 1.9% previously. While core prices are still keeping below the 2% threshold for now, the direction of travel isn't exactly what policymakers would like to see. For now, the ECB could still be afforded some room to be patient after having already raised interest rates twice this summer. The question now is whether the recent inflation surge warrants another move sooner rather than later. So, the central bank definitely cannot afford to be complacent either. If higher energy prices start feeding more evidently into services and wages, then the case for another rate hike in December will only grow stronger.

title: Macro pulse: Treasury yields may be falling for now, but borrowing costs are still painfully high
body: It's been quite a messy reaction in the bond market after the hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday. 10-year Treasury yields briefly pushed above 5.30% on the initial reaction before falling back now to around 5.10%, its lowest in three weeks. That's certainly a welcome change for broader markets, but it doesn't really change things all too much for the US economy. The fact of the matter is just because borrowing costs are getting a little cheaper doesn't exactly mean that they are actually cheap. Think about it this way. Just imagine that you're looking to buy a house and the bank offers you a mortgage at 7%. A few weeks later, that rate drops to 6.9%. Sure, that's a better situation on paper. However, does it suddenly make that dream home affordable? Probably not. And that's essentially the crux of the problem for the US economy. 10-year Treasury yields serve as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy. That goes from mortgage rates to corporate loans and also other forms of long-term financing. Even if these numbers don't move in lockstep with yields, they are still very much influenced by the swings in the bond market. When yields start to move higher as they have been in the past few months, the impact of that trickles all the way down the economic ladder. For businesses, that could mean needing to put expansion plans on hold.

title: US August business inventories +0.4% vs +0.4% expected
body: Prior was +0.8% Retail inventories ex-autos vs +0.8% prior For background, the US business inventories report, formally the Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales release, is published monthly by the Census Bureau about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventory and sales data from three sectors: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers. Together they cover the bulk of goods held in the US economy. By the time the report is released, much of it is already known. Manufacturing inventories come out earlier in the factory orders report. Advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories arrive in the Advance Economic Indicators release roughly four weeks after month end. Business inventories completes the picture, adding the final retail figures and the combined total, which is why it rarely moves markets. The key figures are the monthly change in total inventories and the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how many months it would take to sell existing stock at the current pace of sales. A rising ratio can signal weakening demand or deliberate stockpiling. A falling ratio suggests lean shelves and the potential need to restock. The report's main value is for GDP tracking. Changes in private inventories are one of the most volatile components of quarterly growth and can swing the headline number by a percentage point or more. Economists use the monthly data, particularly retail inventories excluding autos, to refine their GDP estimates.

title: Canada August manufacturing sales +1.5% vs +1.1% expected
body: Prior was -0.4% (revised to -0.3%) Wholesale trade -1.6% vs -1.5% expected Prior trade +0.3% (revised to +0.4%) Statistics Canada publishes two monthly reports that track activity in the goods-producing side of the economy: the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey. Both arrive first as advance "flash" estimates, roughly three weeks after the reference month ends. Full releases follow a few weeks later with detailed industry and provincial breakdowns. Manufacturing sales measure the value of goods shipped by Canadian factories. Key industries include petroleum and coal products, food, transportation equipment, primary metals and chemicals. Because the headline is reported in current dollars, swings in commodity prices can distort the picture, particularly through refined petroleum and metals. Markets and economists pay close attention to the constant-dollar, or volume, figure, which strips out price effects and offers a cleaner read on real output. The report also includes inventories, new orders and unfilled orders, giving a sense of where production is headed. Wholesale trade measures sales by businesses that buy goods and resell them to retailers, other businesses and institutions. It covers sectors such as food and beverages, motor vehicles and parts, machinery and equipment, building materials and personal and household goods.

Where the CPI tracks inflation from the consumer's side of the register, the PPI looks at it from the seller's side, capturing prices at the wholesale and business level before they reach households. The headline figure is the final demand index, which BLS adopted in 2014 to replace the older finished goods measure. It covers goods, services and construction sold for personal consumption, capital investment, government and export. Services make up roughly two-thirds of the index, so it's far more than a gauge of factory-gate prices. Because food and energy prices swing sharply month to month, markets focus on core measures. One strips out food and energy. The narrower ex-food, energy and trade measure also removes trade services. Trade services track changes in retailer and wholesaler margins, which can be volatile and don't always reflect underlying cost pressure.

title: Why do altcoins crash so much harder than Bitcoin?
body: When you look at your screener and notice that Bitcoin is down 5%, you will more often than not also catch that smaller cryptocurrencies are plunging by 10% or even 20%. They are all part of the same crypto market, so it is natural to expect the direction of travel to be the same. But why is the magnitude of the moves so stark? Well, the important difference is more in how these cryptocurrencies trade. Just think of an example where you are trying to sell a second-hand Toyota Corolla. It's a fairly popular car, so chances are you'll easily find someone willing to buy it without having to knock too much your asking price. But now, imagine that you are trying to sell a heavily customised sports car instead. Sure, the car is worth more than the Toyota Corolla and by quite a fair bit for sure. But then, how many people are actually to buy that exact car with such a niche set of specifications? Probably not very many. And if there is a sudden need to sell the car by tomorrow, you might very well have to let it go at a hefty discount in order to find someone that might be interested in buying. So, how does this tie back to the crypto market? With Bitcoin, there's generally a much bigger crowd of people looking to buy and sell. So even when investors start selling, there's a better chance of finding someone who would be willing to buy at a price close to the current market value. As for smaller altcoins, it isn't quite the same story.

title: USDCHF backs away from key daily resistance. Sellers push toward an important hourly floor.
body: The USDCHF moved to a new high yesterday going back to May 2025, but the buyers ran into a key technical target on the daily chart. The 50% midpoint of the move down from the 2025 high comes in at 0.8400. Yesterday's high reached approximately 0.83944, just short of that midpoint. Sellers leaned against the level, and the price rotated lower. The buyers had their shot at extending the rally. They could not get through the next major target. That gives the sellers a level to define risk against on the daily chart. That level remains going forward. Stay below 0.8400, and there is room for a further corrective move lower. A move above—and the ability to stay above—would be needed to open the door for another extension to the upside. The daily chart puts the pullback in perspective Although the rejection is meaningful, the daily chart also shows that the USDCHF has made progress to the upside over recent months. The price moved above its 100-day and 200-day moving averages and worked its way through prior swing levels. The question now is how much of that progress the buyers can hold. Below the current price, the 38.2% retracement of the broader decline is at 0.82116. That sits near the upper end of a daily swing area between approximately 0.81706 and 0.82148. That area becomes important if the selling gathers momentum. Below it, the rising 100-day moving average near 0.81156 provides another longer-term reference.

title: Short covering is driving price action in markets today
body: I hate to break up the party from this nice bounce in equities but when you drill into what's driving it, there's a problem. The biggest gainers today are many of the worst performers this year. That suggests today's move is more driven by short covering than by a rethink on AI or even the reversal in yields. One of the biggest gainers today is Nike, which is up 6.5% while Lululemon is up 6.3%. Both have been among the worst performers this year. Intuit and Expedia are also big gainers. There are some indications that the break lower in yields is part of the equation with housing-related names like Pool Corp up 8% and Zillow up 10.2%. The home builders XHB ETF is also up 2.9%. You could extend that to the whole move but I'd be reluctant to do that. Adding to that sentiment is the ongoing dive in yields, which might suggest that money is being parked in Treasuries instead. At times, you see counter-trend moves like this when funds take down exposure and their shorts are more-thinly traded. There are rumors that the VARA AI fund has blow up and that could be creating a broader de-risking move. Now some have indicated the fund run by Ben Hoskin and David Field has $40 billion AUM, so it could be material. We could also be seeing the post-Leopold playbook unfold. After it was revealed that the heavy selling in AI names was due to Situational Awareness blowing up, then longs piled back in. News like that highlights that the coast is clear on forced selling.
